scope: Bounded non-England revalidation of Norse Greenland. The archaeological and demographic evidence is useful as a hostile-island validation case, but it does not provide a closed same-boundary local-food capacity interval or an EU5 polygon.

promotion_audit.decision: No new quantitative anchor is promoted. Greenland remains validation-only and explicitly rejected for training until its settlement polygon, local-food fraction and independent capacity endpoint are resolved.
promotion_audit.review_method: Triangulated the peer-reviewed human-ecology synthesis, Greenland biological-anthropological study, Vatnahverfi archaeological survey and diet/subsistence review. Population is retained only as an observed historical interval; no capacity is inferred from it.
promotion_audit.reason_not_promoted: The 1,400-2,200 peak estimate is a whole-colony demographic reconstruction, while the EU5 selectors represent game provinces rather than the Eastern and Western Norse settlement polygons. Marine-food substitution, overseas walrus/ivory trade, cooling and settlement abandonment make local-food share and saturation unresolved. A larger 4,000-6,000 model envelope exists in the literature, so treating the low demographic estimate as a ceiling would be false precision.
required_followup: Reconstruct the Eastern and Western Settlement archaeological polygons and intersect them with calibrated EU5 geometry; do not score gardr or herjolfnes province as a colony proxy.
Recover a dated food-balance or sustainable-population interval for the same settlement boundary, separating imported/traded goods from locally produced pastoral and marine foods.
Resolve the competing population model envelopes (approximately 1,400-2,200, 2,000-3,000 and 4,000-6,000) before any upper-capacity claim.
Keep cooling, sea-ice, Thule interaction, walrus trade and abandonment as explicit validation shocks rather than fitting a regional correction.

records.label: Norse Greenland c.1290-1340: hostile settlement validation recheck
records.interval_semantics: Lynnerup's demographic reconstruction, as summarized by Jackson, Dugmore and McGovern, places the whole Norse colony near 1,400-2,200 at its AD 1300 peak. This is an observed population interval, not a local-food capacity interval. No saturation fraction is assigned because marine-food dependence, overseas exchange and the competing higher population models are unresolved.
pressure_evidence: The human-ecology synthesis describes an exceptionally labor-intensive socialized agricultural niche, limited standing timber and scheduling pressure on farms and hunting resources.
Zooarchaeological evidence records increased reliance on migratory harp seals from about AD 1300, consistent with pastoral and winter-fodder constraints but not a quantified saturation fraction.
Vatnahverfi survey work documents extensive Norse farm settlement and later abandonment, providing a physical pressure/feasibility check rather than a colony-wide carrying-capacity estimate.
Diet/subsistence synthesis identifies pastoral livestock, marine mammals and fish, limited barley and local hunting; the mix changed through time and is not a closed calorie balance.
shock_flags: cooling and sea-ice variability in and after the benchmark window
increasing harp-seal dependence and uncertain marine access
walrus ivory and other overseas trade links
Thule interaction and post-1400 settlement abandonment
whole-colony demographic reconstruction rather than an enumeration
records.trade_dependence: mixed; local pastoral and marine foods were substantial, but overseas walrus/ivory exchange and imported materials/food exposure are unresolved
records.food_regime: hay-fed cattle, sheep, goats and horses; limited barley; seals, fish and other marine foods; local hunting
records.boundary_description: Eastern and Western Norse settlements in southwest Greenland, including the archaeological farm zones rather than the full Greenland island or a modern EU5 province
records.source_family_independence: Not independent of the existing Greenland packet: this is an explicit source-and-boundary revalidation that prevents the demographic interval from being misused as a capacity target.
citation_details: Jackson, Dugmore and McGovern, Disequilibrium, Adaptation, and the Norse Settlement of Greenland (Human Ecology 2018), abstract and discussion: the Lynnerup 2014 model peaks near 1,400-2,200 around AD 1300; the paper describes labor demand, resource diversification and increased harp-seal reliance.

Lynnerup, The Greenland Norse: A Biological-Anthropological Study, Meddelelser om Grønland 1998, population-model discussion: approximately 26,000 person-years over 500 years and an average of about 1,400; model envelopes are not a carrying-capacity ceiling.
Krogh/Vatnahverfi archaeological survey record, Meddelelser om Grønland: inland Eastern Settlement farms, site survey and abandonment evidence; no colony-wide population or saturation endpoint.

Arneborg, Lynnerup and Heinemeier, Human Diet and Subsistence Patterns in Norse Greenland AD c.980-c.1450: local pastoral and marine foods plus changing diet, with unresolved trade and climate effects.

Buckland et al., A multiple profile approach to the palynological reconstruction of Norse landscapes in Greenland (Quaternary Research 2014), Eastern Settlement environmental evidence; supports ecological pressure context but not a population-capacity label.
records.notes: This packet closes a recurrent misuse: Greenland's 1,400-2,200 observed population is not silently converted into a capacity floor or ceiling. It remains a held-out hostile-island diagnostic until the same-boundary food balance and EU5 crosswalk are closed.
